topics.h: To dig a well from Delhi to the centre of the Earth, you would have to dig more than 6,000 km. Nobody has dug even 13 km! So how do we know what is inside?
p: The Earth has three main layers: the crust (outermost), the mantle (middle) and the core (centre).
The crust is the thin, rocky skin we live on. It is thinnest under the oceans (about 5 km) and much thicker under the continents, thickest below big mountains like the Himalayas.
Continental crust is mostly silica and alumina (called sial). Oceanic crust is mostly silica and magnesium (called sima). The core is mostly nickel and iron (called nife).

The mantle goes down to about 2,900 km. It is the largest layer by volume. The upper part of the mantle that is weak and slowly flowing is called the asthenosphere; the crust and the rigid top of the mantle together form the lithosphere.
The core has a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Scientists learnt this from earthquake (seismic) waves: S waves cannot travel through liquids, and they do not pass through the outer core.

ex.q: Think it through: The deepest hole ever drilled is only about 12 km deep. How can scientists still say the outer core is liquid?
st: Earthquakes send seismic waves through the whole Earth, and seismographs around the world record them.
P waves can move through solids and liquids, but S waves can move only through solids.
S waves are not recorded on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, because they are stopped at the outer core.
So the outer core must be liquid. These indirect clues, along with meteorites, volcanoes and gravity readings, tell us about the inside.
ex.a: By studying how seismic waves travel; S waves cannot pass through the outer core, so it must be liquid.

topics.rl: Think of a mango: the thin skin is like the crust, the thick juicy pulp is like the mantle and the hard seed is like the core.

topics.h: Look at a world map: the bulge of Brazil seems to fit into the curve of West Africa like jigsaw pieces. Is that just luck?
p: In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the continental drift theory: all continents were once joined in one supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by a huge ocean called Panthalassa.
Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, which later broke into today's continents. India was part of Gondwanaland.

Evidence: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit; rocks of the same age match across the Atlantic; fossils of the same reptile, Mesosaurus, are found in both South Africa and Brazil; old glacial deposits (tillite) are found in India and other southern lands.

Plate tectonics explains the movement: the lithosphere is broken into large plates that move slowly, a few centimetres a year, over the asthenosphere. There are seven major plates and many minor ones.

Plates meet at three kinds of boundaries: divergent (move apart, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge), convergent (move towards each other, e.g. Himalayas) and transform (slide past each other, e.g. San Andreas Fault).

ex.q: Think it through: Why are the Himalayas called young fold mountains that are still rising?
st: The Indian plate broke away from Gondwanaland and moved north towards Asia.
When the Indian plate pushed into the Eurasian plate, the layers of rock and sea-floor sediment between them were squeezed and folded upwards.
This happened only tens of millions of years ago, which is recent in the Earth's history, so the Himalayas are young.
The Indian plate is still pushing north, so the Himalayas are still rising and the region still has earthquakes.
ex.a: Because they formed recently from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, which is still going on.

topics.rl: The Himalayas, the earthquakes in north and north-east India, and even fossils of sea shells found high up in the Himalayas are all results of moving plates.

topics.h: The Earth shakes many times every day, but most quakes are so tiny that only machines notice them. What makes the ground shake?
p: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground. It happens when rocks along a fault, usually near plate boundaries, suddenly slip and release stored energy.
The point inside the Earth where the slip starts is the focus (hypocentre). The point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre, where shaking is usually strongest.
Energy travels as seismic waves: P waves arrive first, then S waves, and surface waves arrive last and do the most damage.
A seismograph records the waves. Magnitude (energy released) is measured on the Richter scale; intensity (damage and shaking felt) on the Mercalli scale, which runs from 1 to 12.
The Himalayan region, the north-east and the Kachchh region of Gujarat are among the most earthquake-prone parts of India. A strong earthquake struck Bhuj in Gujarat on 26 January 2001.

ex.q: Think it through: Your school is in an earthquake-prone town. When the shaking starts, what should you do and why?
st: Do not run out while the ground is shaking, because falling objects and glass are the biggest danger.
DROP to your knees, take COVER under a strong desk and HOLD ON to it until the shaking stops.
Keep away from windows, shelves and anything that can fall. Do not use the lift.
When the shaking stops, walk out calmly with your teacher to an open ground away from buildings, trees and electric wires.
ex.a: Drop, cover and hold on until the shaking stops, then move calmly to an open area.

topics.rl: Schools in India hold earthquake drills, and engineers design earthquake-resistant buildings with strong frames for hilly and quake-prone areas.

topics.h: India has an active volcano! It sits on an island in the Andaman Sea and has puffed out ash even in this century.
p: A volcano is an opening (vent) in the crust through which molten rock, gases, ash and rock pieces come out. Molten rock is called magma below the surface and lava once it comes out.
Volcanoes can be active (erupting now or recently), dormant (quiet for a long time but may erupt again) or extinct (not expected to erupt again).
Most volcanoes are near plate boundaries. The 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean has many active volcanoes and earthquakes.
Barren Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands is India's only active volcano.
Lava builds new land. The Deccan Traps of Maharashtra were formed by huge lava flows from cracks; the basalt rock broke down into fertile black soil, which is good for cotton.

ex.q: Think it through: Volcanoes can be dangerous, yet many farmers live on their slopes. Why?
st: Volcanic ash and lava contain many minerals.
Over time they break down into very fertile soil that grows good crops.
Volcanic areas can also give hot springs and geothermal energy, and valuable minerals.
So people accept the risk, and scientists watch active volcanoes to warn them before an eruption.
ex.a: Volcanic material forms very fertile soil, and volcanoes also provide minerals and geothermal energy.

topics.rl: The black soil of Maharashtra and Gujarat that grows cotton comes from ancient lava of the Deccan Traps.

topics.h: You cannot see it, but you are carrying a blanket of air above you that reaches hundreds of kilometres into space. It even keeps meteors from hitting you!
p: The atmosphere is the layer of air held around the Earth by gravity. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen; argon, carbon dioxide and other gases make up the remaining 1% or so. Water vapour and dust are also present in varying amounts.
Troposphere (lowest, about 13 km on average; higher at the equator, lower at the poles): almost all weather, clouds and water vapour are here, and temperature falls as you go up.
Stratosphere (up to about 50 km): contains the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. It has almost no clouds, so its lower part is good for flying aeroplanes.
Mesosphere (up to about 80 km): the coldest layer; meteors burn up here and look like shooting stars.
Thermosphere (about 80 to 400 km) contains the ionosphere, which reflects radio waves back to the Earth. Above it is the exosphere, where the air is extremely thin.

ex.q: Think it through: A pilot flying from Delhi to Kolkata climbs above the clouds and the ride becomes smooth. Which layer is the plane in, and why is it calm?
st: Clouds, rain, storms and most bumpy air movements happen in the troposphere.
Above the troposphere is the stratosphere, which has almost no clouds or weather.
So when the plane rises above the weather into the lower stratosphere, the air is steady.
ex.a: In the lower stratosphere, which is above the clouds and weather of the troposphere.

topics.rl: Doctors advise sunscreen because some UV rays still reach us; the ozone layer stops most of them. The radio you hear and the shooting stars you see on clear nights both depend on layers of the atmosphere.

topics.h: "Carry an umbrella today" is about weather. "Mumbai is warm and humid" is about climate. Can you spot the difference?
p: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place for a short time, like a few hours or a day. It can change quickly.
Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, usually about 30 years or more.
The elements of weather and climate are temperature, air pressure, wind, humidity (water vapour in the air) and precipitation (rain, snow, hail).
Air pressure is highest at sea level and falls with height. Wind blows from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure.

Instruments: thermometer (temperature), barometer (air pressure), anemometer (wind speed), wind vane (wind direction), rain gauge (rainfall) and hygrometer (humidity). The India Meteorological Department (IMD) records weather and issues forecasts.

ex.q: Think it through: On a day in Chennai, the morning is sunny, the afternoon has a thunderstorm and the night is cool. Does Chennai's climate change three times that day?
st: The sunny morning, stormy afternoon and cool night are changes in weather, which can change within hours.
Climate is the average pattern of many years, so one day cannot change it.
Chennai's climate stays the same: warm and humid for most of the year.
ex.a: No. Only the weather changed; climate is the long-term average and does not change in a day.

topics.rl: Farmers watch the weather forecast before sowing or spraying crops, while builders and planners use climate data to design houses and drains.

topics.h: Shimla and Ludhiana are only about 130 km apart as the crow flies, yet in May one is pleasant and the other is baking. Why?
p: Latitude: places near the equator get more direct sunlight and are hot; places towards the poles are cooler. The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India.
Altitude: temperature in the troposphere falls by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m of height, so hill stations like Shimla, Ooty and Darjeeling are cool.
Distance from the sea: the sea keeps coastal places like Mumbai and Chennai moderate (equable). Places far inland like Delhi have extreme (continental) climates with hot summers and cold winters.

Relief and winds: the Himalayas block cold winds from Central Asia and make the monsoon winds shed their rain over India. Windward slopes of mountains get heavy rain; the leeward side stays drier (rain shadow).
Ocean currents also matter: warm currents warm nearby coasts, cold currents cool them. India has a monsoon type of climate; the south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around 1 June.

ex.q: Think it through: A town at the foot of a hill is at 30 °C. What will be the temperature at a hill station 2,000 m higher, using the normal lapse rate?
st: Temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m.
2,000 m is 2 × 1,000 m, so the fall is 2 × 6.5 = 13 °C.

topics.rl: Families from the plains go to Nainital or Munnar in summer to escape the heat, thanks to altitude. Weather apps in Mumbai rarely show the extreme heat that Delhi sees, thanks to the sea.

topics.t: The world ocean and the ocean floor
topics.h: If you dropped Mount Everest into the deepest part of the ocean, its peak would still be under about 2 km of water!
p: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, and about 97% of all the Earth's water is in the salty oceans.
There are five oceans: Pacific (largest and deepest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic (smallest). The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country.
Continental shelf: the shallow, gently sloping edge of a continent under the sea. It is rich in fish and often in oil and gas, like Mumbai High off the coast of Maharashtra.
Continental slope: the steep drop from the shelf to the deep ocean. Deep-sea (abyssal) plains: huge, very flat areas covered with fine sediment.

Trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean; the Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about 11 km deep. Mid-ocean ridges are long underwater mountain chains, seamounts are underwater mountains that do not reach the surface, and atolls are ring-shaped coral islands around a lagoon, like many in Lakshadweep.

ex.q: Think it through: Mount Everest is about 8,849 m high and the deepest point of the Mariana Trench is about 11,000 m deep. Would Everest stick out if placed in the trench?
st: Compare the depth with the height: 11,000 m is more than 8,849 m.
Difference: 11,000 − 8,849 = 2,151 m, which is about 2 km.
So the top of Everest would still be about 2 km under water.
ex.a: No. Its peak would be about 2 km below the sea surface.

topics.rl: Fishing boats from Kerala and Gujarat work mostly over the continental shelf, and the oil rigs of Mumbai High stand on it too.

topics.h: The sea at Puri rises and falls like it is breathing, and its water tastes salty. What makes the ocean salty and restless?
p: Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in sea water. The average salinity of the oceans is about 35 parts per thousand, that is about 35 g of salt in 1,000 g of sea water.

High evaporation raises salinity; fresh water from rivers, rain and melting ice lowers it. The Bay of Bengal is less salty than the Arabian Sea because big rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra pour fresh water into it.
Most waves are made by wind blowing over the water. A tsunami is a series of giant waves usually caused by an earthquake under the sea, like the one on 26 December 2004.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity, helped by the Sun. Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides a day. Spring tides (highest) come at full moon and new moon; neap tides (lowest range) come when the Moon is at its quarters.

Ocean currents are streams of water flowing in a fixed direction. Warm currents flow from near the equator towards the poles (Gulf Stream); cold currents flow from the poles towards the equator (Labrador Current). Where they meet, fog forms and fish are plentiful. Currents in the north Indian Ocean change direction with the monsoon.

ex.q: Think it through: Why are the highest tides seen on full moon and new moon days?
st: Tides are caused by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun pulling on the oceans.
On full moon and new moon days the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a straight line.
Their pulls add together, so high tides are higher and low tides are lower. These are spring tides.
ex.a: Because the Sun, Moon and Earth are in line, so their pulls combine to give spring tides.

topics.rl: Fishers in Odisha and Gujarat plan trips by the tide table, salt pans need sunny weather for evaporation, and ships use tides to enter ports.

topics.h: Every year, lakhs of olive ridley turtles crawl onto the beaches of Odisha to lay their eggs. The ocean is full of such amazing life!
p: Marine life ranges from tiny plankton to the blue whale, the largest animal known. Phytoplankton make food using sunlight, produce a large share of the Earth's oxygen and form the base of ocean food chains.

Coral reefs are built over many years by tiny animals called coral polyps. In India they are found in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Very warm water can make corals lose their colour (bleaching).

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees of coastal swamps with special breathing roots. They protect coasts from storms and erosion and are nurseries for fish. The Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is the largest mangrove forest in the world and a home of the Royal Bengal tiger.

Ocean resources: fish and seafood, salt (Gujarat is India's largest producer), oil and natural gas (Mumbai High), manganese-rich nodules on the deep sea floor, tidal and wave energy, and sea routes for trade. India's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) stretches 200 nautical miles from its coast.
Threats include plastic waste, oil spills, overfishing and warming seas. Seasonal fishing bans in the breeding season, protected marine areas and beach clean-ups help.

ex.q: Think it through: A cyclone hits two villages on the Odisha coast. One has a thick mangrove forest in front of it, the other does not. Which village is likely to suffer less, and why?
st: Mangrove trees have dense roots and branches that slow down waves and storm surges.
Their roots hold the soil and reduce coastal erosion.
So the waves reaching the village behind the mangroves are weaker.
ex.a: The village protected by mangroves, because they slow waves and hold the coast together.

topics.rl: The salt in your kitchen probably came from the salt pans of Gujarat, and the fish curry of Kerala or Bengal depends on healthy seas.

topics.h: Of all the planets we know, only one has mangoes, monsoon frogs and you. What makes the Earth so special?
p: The Earth has four spheres: the lithosphere (rocks, soil and land), the hydrosphere (oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and groundwater), the atmosphere (air) and the biosphere (all living things).
The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and life is possible. It stretches from the deep ocean floor to the lower part of the atmosphere.
The Earth is the only planet known to support life. It is at the right distance from the Sun, so it has liquid water and suitable temperatures, and its atmosphere has oxygen and an ozone layer.
The spheres are linked: plants take carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, roots break rocks and help form soil, and the water cycle connects the oceans, the air and the land.

Living things are called biotic components; non-living things like sunlight, air, water and soil are abiotic components. Human actions like cutting forests and polluting rivers affect all four spheres.

ex.q: Think it through: Look at a village pond with lotus plants, fish and frogs. Which of the four spheres can you find there?
st: The water of the pond belongs to the hydrosphere.
The mud and soil at the bottom and banks belong to the lithosphere.
The air above the water and the air dissolved in it belong to the atmosphere.
The lotus plants, fish, frogs and tiny organisms belong to the biosphere. So all four spheres meet in the pond.
ex.a: All four: hydrosphere, lithosphere, atmosphere and biosphere.

topics.rl: When you plant a sapling on Van Mahotsav, you add to the biosphere and it helps the atmosphere and the soil too.

topics.h: In the grasslands of a national park, a deer eats grass and a tiger hunts the deer. When the tiger dies, mushrooms and bacteria recycle it. Everyone is connected!
p: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings (sunlight, air, water, soil). A pond, a forest and a desert are all ecosystems.

Producers (green plants, algae) make food from sunlight. Consumers eat others: herbivores are primary consumers, carnivores that eat them are secondary consumers, and so on. Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

A food chain shows who eats whom, for example grass → deer → tiger. Many linked food chains form a food web. Energy flows one way from the Sun, and only about 10% passes to the next level, so food chains are short. Nutrients keep cycling.

Ecosystems are terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) or aquatic (freshwater, marine). Large areas with similar climate, plants and animals are called biomes: forest, grassland, desert, aquatic and altitudinal (high mountain) biomes.

ex.q: Think it through: In the food chain grass → deer → tiger, the grass stores 10,000 units of energy. About how much reaches the tiger?
st: Only about 10% of the energy passes from one level to the next.
Grass to deer: 10% of 10,000 = 1,000 units.
Deer to tiger: 10% of 1,000 = 100 units.

topics.rl: A school kitchen garden, a village pond and even a fish tank at home are small ecosystems. Compost pits work because of decomposers.

topics.h: India has more than a thousand varieties of mango, hundreds of kinds of rice and animals found nowhere else on Earth. That variety is called biodiversity.
p: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth. It exists at three levels: genetic diversity (variety within a species, like many types of rice or mango), species diversity and ecosystem diversity.
India is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries. With only about 2.4% of the world's land area, it has about 7 to 8% of the recorded species.

India has parts of four of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands). Endemic species found only in a region include the lion-tailed macaque and the Nilgiri tahr of the Western Ghats.
Threats: loss of habitat as forests are cleared, poaching, pollution, invasive species like lantana and water hyacinth, and climate change.

Conservation: in-situ (in natural homes: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves) and ex-situ (outside: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks). India passed the Wildlife (Protection) Act in 1972 and started Project Tiger in 1973. Communities help too: the Bishnois of Rajasthan protect blackbuck and khejri trees, and in the Chipko movement villagers hugged trees to save them.

ex.q: Think it through: Why does saving the tiger help save the whole forest?
st: A tiger needs a large, healthy forest with plenty of deer and other prey.
To protect tigers, the forest, its grasslands and its water sources must all be protected.
The tiger, as a top predator, also keeps the number of deer in balance, so plants are not overgrazed.
So protecting one tiger protects thousands of other plants and animals in its home.
ex.a: Protecting tigers means protecting their whole habitat, and tigers keep the food web in balance.

topics.rl: When you visit Gir to see the Asiatic lion or Kaziranga to see the one-horned rhinoceros, you are visiting places set up for in-situ conservation.

qa.q: Which is the outermost layer of the Earth?
qa.e: The crust is the thin rocky outer layer on which we live, and it lies above the mantle.

qa.q: Where is the Earth's crust thinnest?
qa.e: Oceanic crust is only about 5 km thick, while continental crust is much thicker, especially under high mountains.

qa.q: The Earth's core is made mainly of which two metals?
qa.e: The core is called nife because it is made mainly of nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe).

qa.q: Which part of the Earth is liquid?
qa.e: The outer core is liquid. The inner core is solid because the huge pressure there keeps it solid even though it is very hot.

qa.q: Which layer of the Earth is the largest by volume?
qa.e: The mantle stretches from below the crust to about 2,900 km deep, so it holds the largest share of the Earth's volume.

qa.q: What is the lithosphere?
qa.a: The crust together with the rigid uppermost part of the mantle
qa.e: The lithosphere is the solid, rigid outer shell: the crust plus the top part of the mantle. It is broken into plates.

qa.q: Why do scientists say S waves prove that the outer core is liquid?
qa.a: S waves cannot travel through liquids, and they do not pass through the outer core
qa.e: S waves move only through solids. Because they are stopped at the outer core, that layer must be liquid.

qa.q: The mantle extends to a depth of about how many kilometres?
qa.e: The mantle begins below the crust and continues to about 2,900 km, where the outer core starts.

qa.q: What name did Wegener give to the single supercontinent that once existed?
qa.e: Pangaea means 'all earth'. Panthalassa, meaning 'all water', was the ocean around it.

qa.q: India was once part of which southern landmass?
qa.e: Gondwanaland was the southern part of Pangaea and included India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.

qa.q: Which of these is evidence for continental drift?
qa.a: Fossils of the same reptile, Mesosaurus, in South Africa and Brazil
qa.e: A small freshwater reptile could not cross an ocean, so finding its fossils on both sides shows the continents were once joined.

qa.q: At a divergent boundary, the plates:
qa.e: At divergent boundaries plates pull apart and new crust forms from rising magma, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

qa.q: The Himalayas were formed mainly by:
qa.a: the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate
qa.e: The Indian plate moved north and pushed into the Eurasian plate. The rock layers between them folded up to form the Himalayas.

qa.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is an example of which kind of plate boundary?
qa.e: Along the San Andreas Fault the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other sideways, which is a transform boundary.

qa.q: About how fast do tectonic plates usually move?
qa.e: Plates move very slowly, usually a few centimetres a year, but over millions of years this adds up to thousands of kilometres.

qa.q: How many major tectonic plates is the lithosphere usually divided into?
qa.e: The lithosphere has seven major plates, such as the Pacific, Eurasian and Indo-Australian plates, plus several minor plates.

qa.q: The place inside the Earth where an earthquake starts is called the:
qa.e: The focus, or hypocentre, is the point underground where rocks first slip. The epicentre is on the surface above it.

qa.q: Where is the shaking of an earthquake usually strongest?
qa.e: The epicentre is the surface point closest to the focus, so the waves reach it with the most energy.

qa.q: Which seismic waves cause the most damage on the surface?
qa.e: Surface waves travel along the ground, arrive last and shake buildings the most.

qa.q: Which instrument records earthquake waves?
qa.e: A seismograph records the waves produced by an earthquake. A barometer measures air pressure.

qa.q: On the Richter scale, each step up of 1 means the ground motion recorded is how many times larger?
qa.e: The Richter scale goes up in steps of ten: a magnitude 6 earthquake makes waves 10 times larger than a magnitude 5 one.

qa.q: Most earthquakes happen:
qa.e: Plates push, pull or slide along their edges, so stress builds up and is released there as earthquakes.

qa.q: During an earthquake you are inside a classroom. What is the safest thing to do?
qa.a: Get under a strong desk and hold on
qa.e: Drop, cover and hold on protects you from falling objects. Running, windows and lifts are all dangerous during shaking.

qa.q: Which part of India is among the most earthquake-prone?
qa.e: The Himalayas lie where the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate, so the region has frequent earthquakes.

qa.q: What is lava?
qa.a: Molten rock that has come out on the Earth's surface
qa.e: Molten rock is called magma while it is underground and lava once it pours out on the surface.

qa.q: Where is India's only active volcano?
qa.a: Barren Island, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
qa.e: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano. The others listed are mountains, not active volcanoes.

qa.q: A volcano that has not erupted for a very long time but may erupt again is called:
qa.e: Dormant means 'sleeping'. An extinct volcano is not expected to erupt again at all.

qa.q: The 'Ring of Fire' is found around which ocean?
qa.e: Many plate boundaries surround the Pacific Ocean, so it is ringed by volcanoes and earthquake zones.

qa.q: The Deccan Traps were formed by:
qa.a: huge flows of lava that spread over the land
qa.e: Long ago, lava poured out of cracks again and again and hardened into thick layers of basalt called the Deccan Traps.

qa.q: Black soil, good for growing cotton, formed mainly from which rock?
qa.e: Black soil (regur) formed from the weathering of basalt of the Deccan Traps.

qa.q: Why are most volcanoes found near plate boundaries?
qa.a: Magma rises more easily where plates pull apart or one plate sinks under another
qa.e: At plate boundaries the crust is cracked or melting, which gives magma a path to the surface.

qa.q: Which of these is a benefit of volcanoes?
qa.e: Volcanic ash forms rich soil, and the heat below volcanic areas can be used as geothermal energy.

qa.q: About what percentage of dry air is nitrogen?
qa.e: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of dry air, oxygen about 21% and the other gases together about 1%.

qa.q: In which layer do clouds, rain and storms mostly form?
qa.e: The troposphere holds almost all the water vapour and dust, so weather happens there.

qa.q: The ozone layer protects us by absorbing:
qa.e: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays.

qa.q: Shooting stars are meteors burning up in which layer?
qa.e: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere, about 50 to 80 km above the Earth.

qa.q: Which part of the atmosphere reflects radio waves back to the Earth?
qa.e: The ionosphere, within the thermosphere, has charged particles that bounce radio waves back to the Earth.

qa.q: What generally happens to temperature as you go higher in the troposphere?
qa.e: Air in the troposphere is heated mainly from the ground, so it gets colder with height. That is why hill stations are cool.

qa.q: Why is the lower stratosphere suitable for flying aeroplanes?
qa.a: It has almost no clouds or weather disturbances
qa.e: Above the troposphere there are hardly any clouds or storms, so flights are smoother.

qa.q: What holds the atmosphere around the Earth?
qa.e: The Earth's gravity pulls the gases of the atmosphere towards it, so they do not escape into space.

qa.q: Which statement describes climate rather than weather?
qa.a: Kerala receives heavy rain every monsoon season
qa.e: Climate is the usual pattern over many years. The other statements describe conditions for a short time.

qa.q: Climate is usually worked out from weather records of about how many years or more?
qa.e: Climate is the average of weather over a long period, usually about 30 years or more.

qa.q: Which instrument measures air pressure?
qa.e: A barometer measures air pressure. A falling barometer reading often warns of stormy weather.

qa.q: An anemometer is used to measure:
qa.e: The spinning cups of an anemometer turn faster in stronger wind. Wind direction is shown by a wind vane.

qa.q: Wind blows from:
qa.a: high pressure areas to low pressure areas
qa.e: Air moves from where pressure is higher to where it is lower, just like air rushing out of a pumped-up balloon.

qa.q: Humidity means:
qa.a: the amount of water vapour in the air
qa.e: Humidity tells us how much water vapour the air holds. High humidity makes us feel sticky, as in coastal cities.

qa.q: Where is air pressure highest?
qa.e: At sea level there is the most air pressing down from above, so pressure is highest. It falls as we go up.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an element of weather?
qa.e: Temperature, air pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation are the elements of weather. Soil is part of the land, not the atmosphere.

qa.q: Ooty is much cooler than Chennai in summer mainly because of its:
qa.e: Ooty is high up in the Nilgiri Hills. Temperature falls with height, so it is cooler.

qa.q: A place at sea level has a temperature of 30 °C. Using a fall of 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, what is the temperature at 2,000 m (in °C)?
qa.e: The fall is 2 × 6.5 = 13 °C, so the temperature is 30 − 13 = 17 °C.

qa.q: Why does Delhi have hotter summers and colder winters than Mumbai?
qa.a: Delhi is far from the moderating effect of the sea
qa.e: The sea heats and cools slowly and keeps Mumbai's temperatures moderate. Delhi, far inland, has an extreme climate.

qa.q: How do the Himalayas affect India's climate?
qa.a: They block cold Central Asian winds and help the monsoon winds bring rain to India
qa.e: The Himalayas act as a wall: they keep out icy winds in winter and trap the monsoon winds so they rain over India.

qa.q: Which place is known for receiving the highest average rainfall in the world?
qa.e: Mawsynram in Meghalaya, in the Khasi Hills, receives the highest average rainfall in the world.

qa.q: The leeward side of a mountain range usually:
qa.a: gets less rain and is called a rain shadow area
qa.e: Moist winds drop most rain on the windward side as they rise. Air coming down the far side is drier.

qa.q: The south-west monsoon normally arrives in Kerala around:
qa.e: The usual onset date of the south-west monsoon over Kerala is around 1 June, and it then spreads across India.

qa.q: Which latitude line passes through the middle of India?
qa.e: The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′ N) divides India into a southern tropical part and a northern subtropical part. Mainland India lies roughly between 8° N and 37° N.

qa.q: Which is the largest and deepest ocean?
qa.e: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean and also has the deepest point, in the Mariana Trench.

qa.q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
qa.e: About 71% of the surface is water and about 29% is land. The figure 97% is the share of all water that is in the oceans.

qa.q: The deepest known part of the ocean is in the:
qa.e: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific is about 11 km deep, the deepest place known in the oceans.

qa.q: Which part of the ocean floor is the shallowest and lies next to the land?
qa.e: The continental shelf is the submerged edge of the continent. The ocean gets deeper along the slope and is deepest in trenches.

qa.q: Mumbai High, an important source of oil and natural gas, lies on the:
qa.a: continental shelf of the Arabian Sea
qa.e: Mumbai High is an offshore oil field on the shallow continental shelf west of Mumbai, in the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: What is an atoll?
qa.a: A ring-shaped coral island or reef around a lagoon
qa.e: Atolls are built by corals and form a ring around a shallow lagoon. Many of the Lakshadweep islands are coral atolls.

qa.q: Which is the only ocean named after a country?
qa.e: The Indian Ocean is named after India, the only ocean named after a country.

qa.q: An underwater mountain that rises from the sea floor but does not reach the surface is a:
qa.e: A seamount is usually an old volcano under the sea. A flat-topped seamount is called a guyot.

qa.q: The average salinity of ocean water is about how many parts per thousand?
qa.e: On average, 1,000 g of sea water contains about 35 g of dissolved salts.

qa.q: What mainly causes tides?
qa.a: The pull of the Moon's gravity on the oceans
qa.e: The Moon's gravity pulls the ocean water, helped by the Sun, creating the regular rise and fall of the tides.

qa.q: Spring tides occur:
qa.a: on full moon and new moon days
qa.e: At full moon and new moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line and their pulls add up, giving the highest tides.

qa.q: Most ordinary sea waves are produced by:
qa.e: Wind drags the surface water and builds up waves. Stronger winds make bigger waves.

qa.q: A tsunami is usually caused by:
qa.e: A sudden movement of the sea floor during an undersea earthquake pushes up huge amounts of water and creates a tsunami.

qa.q: The Gulf Stream is an example of:
qa.e: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from near the equator across the Atlantic towards north-western Europe.

qa.q: Which of these increases the salinity of sea water?
qa.a: High evaporation in hot, dry areas
qa.e: Evaporation removes water but leaves the salt behind, so the remaining water becomes saltier.

qa.q: Why is the Bay of Bengal less salty than the Arabian Sea?
qa.a: Large rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra pour fresh water into it
qa.e: The Bay of Bengal receives huge amounts of river water, which dilutes the salt in it.

qa.q: What forms the base of most ocean food chains?
qa.e: Phytoplankton are tiny plant-like organisms that make food using sunlight. Almost all other sea creatures depend on them directly or indirectly.

qa.q: Which is the largest animal known to have lived on the Earth?
qa.e: The blue whale is larger than any dinosaur known. Surprisingly, it feeds on tiny shrimp-like krill.

qa.q: Coral reefs are built by:
qa.a: tiny sea animals called coral polyps
qa.e: Coral polyps make hard skeletons of calcium carbonate. Over many years these build up into reefs.

qa.q: Which of these is a coral reef area of India?
qa.e: India's main coral reefs are in the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kachchh, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The others are lakes.

qa.q: The Sundarbans are best known as:
qa.a: the largest mangrove forest in the world, home of the Royal Bengal tiger
qa.e: The Sundarbans lie in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, shared by India and Bangladesh.

qa.q: How do mangrove forests help coastal people?
qa.a: They reduce damage from storm waves and slow down coastal erosion
qa.e: Mangroves slow down waves and their roots hold the soil, protecting the coast. They are also breeding grounds for fish.

qa.q: India's Exclusive Economic Zone extends up to how many nautical miles from the coast?
qa.e: In its EEZ, up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, India has rights over fish, oil, gas and minerals. 12 nautical miles is the limit of territorial waters.

qa.q: Why is a fishing ban followed along India's coasts for some weeks every year?
qa.a: To let fish breed and keep fish stocks healthy
qa.e: The ban falls in the breeding season so that young fish can grow, which prevents overfishing.

qa.q: What is the biosphere?
qa.a: The zone of the Earth where land, water and air meet and life exists
qa.e: The biosphere is the life zone, where the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere interact to support living things.

qa.q: Mountains, rocks and soil are part of the:
qa.e: 'Litho' means stone. The lithosphere is the solid outer part of the Earth, including landforms and soil.

qa.q: Oceans, rivers, glaciers and groundwater together form the:
qa.e: 'Hydro' means water. All the water on the Earth, liquid or frozen, makes up the hydrosphere.

qa.q: Why is the Earth able to support life?
qa.a: It has liquid water, suitable temperatures and air with oxygen
qa.e: The Earth's distance from the Sun gives temperatures at which water stays liquid, and its atmosphere has oxygen and protective ozone.

qa.q: Which of these is a biotic component?
qa.e: Biotic means living. Earthworms are living things; sunlight, water and sand are abiotic (non-living).

qa.q: How do green plants change the atmosphere?
qa.a: They take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
qa.e: In photosynthesis, plants use carbon dioxide and release oxygen, linking the biosphere with the atmosphere.

qa.q: Which example shows the biosphere changing the lithosphere?
qa.a: Roots of a peepal tree cracking a rock
qa.e: Roots are living (biosphere) and they break rock (lithosphere). The other examples do not involve living things.

qa.q: The biosphere reaches from the deep ocean floor up to the:
qa.e: Living things are found from the deepest seas to the lower atmosphere, where birds, insects and spores can float. Higher up the air is too thin and cold.

qa.q: What is an ecosystem?
qa.a: Living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings
qa.e: An ecosystem includes both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) parts and the way they interact.

qa.q: Which of these is a producer?
qa.e: Green plants like the neem tree make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers. A mushroom is a fungus, a decomposer.

qa.q: What is the role of decomposers such as bacteria and fungi?
qa.a: They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil
qa.e: Decomposers recycle nutrients. Without them, dead material would pile up and soil would lose its nutrients.

qa.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog is a:
qa.e: The grasshopper eats grass (primary consumer). The frog eats the grasshopper, so it is a secondary consumer.

qa.q: In grass → deer → tiger, the grass has 10,000 units of energy. With about 10% passed on at each step, how many units reach the tiger?
qa.e: Grass to deer: 10% of 10,000 = 1,000. Deer to tiger: 10% of 1,000 = 100.

qa.q: What is the main source of energy for almost all ecosystems?
qa.e: Producers capture sunlight to make food, and that energy then passes along the food chain.

qa.q: Which of these is an aquatic ecosystem?
qa.e: Aquatic ecosystems are water-based, like ponds, lakes, rivers and seas. The others are terrestrial (land-based).

qa.q: Why are most food chains short, with only 3 to 5 levels?
qa.a: Most energy is lost at each level, so little is left for higher levels
qa.e: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level, so after a few steps there is too little to support another level.

qa.q: What does biodiversity mean?
qa.a: The variety of all living things in an area or on Earth
qa.e: Biodiversity covers the variety of genes, species and ecosystems.

qa.q: Farmers in India grow hundreds of varieties of rice. Which level of biodiversity does this show?
qa.e: All rice varieties belong to the same species; the differences between them are genetic diversity.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of in-situ conservation?
qa.e: In-situ means 'in the original place'. National parks protect plants and animals in their natural habitat. The others are ex-situ.

qa.q: Where are Asiatic lions found in the wild today?
qa.e: The Gir forest and nearby areas of Gujarat are the only place in the world where Asiatic lions live in the wild.

qa.q: Which of these is a biodiversity hotspot that lies partly in India?
qa.e: The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka hotspot is rich in species found nowhere else. India also has parts of the Himalaya, Indo-Burma and Sundaland hotspots.

qa.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched in India?
qa.e: Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats. Project Elephant began later, in 1992.

qa.q: Which of these is a major threat to biodiversity?
qa.a: Clearing forests for new farms and roads
qa.e: Habitat loss is one of the biggest threats, because plants and animals lose their homes and food.

qa.q: The Chipko movement is remembered because villagers:
qa.a: hugged trees to stop them from being cut down
qa.e: In the Chipko movement of the 1970s in the Himalayan region of present-day Uttarakhand, villagers, many of them women, hugged trees to prevent felling.
